ToolHeader.title: JWT Decoder — see what is inside a token
ToolHeader.description: Open a JSON Web Token: header, payload and expiry. Everything runs in your browser and nothing is sent anywhere.

Summary.title: This token
Summary.empty: Paste a token — everything inside it appears here
Summary.privacy: The token never leaves your browser
Summary.unsigned: This token's header says alg: none, meaning it is not signed at all. If a server trusts the algorithm named in the header, anyone can mint a token like this. It is the oldest JWT attack there is.

status.noExpiry: No expiry claim — this token does not expire on its own

header.title: Header
header.description: States which algorithm signed the token and what kind of token it is. Signed, but not encrypted.

payload.title: Payload
payload.description: The token's contents — its claims. Also not encrypted: anyone can read it, which is why passwords and secrets never go here.

signature.title: Signature
signature.description: The third segment — a signature over the header and payload. This tool neither decodes nor verifies it: verifying needs the server's secret, and a secret should never be typed into a web page.

Errors.threeParts: A JWT is three dot-separated segments: header.payload.signature
Errors.notBase64: The {part} segment is not base64url — part of it may have been lost when copying.
Errors.notJson: The {part} segment decoded, but what came out was not JSON.
Errors.notObject: The {part} segment is not a JSON object.
Errors.tooLarge: That file is too large. A JWT is a few kilobytes at most.
Errors.unsupported: That file type is not supported. Only .txt and .json.
Errors.unreadable: The file could not be read.

reference.title: How a JWT is built
reference.intro: A JSON Web Token is three base64url segments separated by dots. The first two are plain JSON: they are signed but NOT encrypted, so anyone holding the token can read what is inside. The signature only proves the token has not been altered.

header.title: Header
header.body: Which algorithm signed it (alg) and what kind of token it is (typ). Sometimes a key id — kid — lives here too.

payload.title: Payload
payload.body: The claims: who, for whom, until when. Plain text, which is why secrets never belong here.

signature.title: Signature
signature.body: A signature over the header and payload, made with a shared secret or a private key. It alone proves the token is genuine.

iss.name: Issuer
iss.meaning: Who issued the token — usually the auth server's URL. The receiving side checks it against an allow-list.

sub.name: Subject
sub.meaning: Who the token is about. In most systems an internal user id rather than an email, because emails change.

aud.name: Audience
aud.meaning: Who the token is for. Checked so one service does not accept another service's token.

exp.name: Expiration Time
exp.meaning: After this moment the token must not be accepted. Seconds since the epoch.

nbf.name: Not Before
nbf.meaning: The token is not yet in force until this moment. Rarely used.

iat.name: Issued At
iat.meaning: When the token was issued. Together with `exp` it gives the token's lifetime.

jti.name: JWT ID
jti.meaning: A unique id for the token, used to stop the same one being replayed.

what.question: Is a JWT encrypted? Can anyone read the payload?
what.answer: A JWT is signed, not encrypted. The header and payload are plain base64url, so anyone holding the token can decode and read them in a second. The signature guarantees exactly one thing: that the token has not been altered in transit. That is why passwords, card numbers and other secrets never go in the payload.

verify.question: Does this tool verify the signature?
verify.answer: No, and that is deliberate. Verifying needs the server's shared secret (for HS256) or its public key (for RS256). Typing a shared secret into a web page is the easiest way to leak it, even if the page sends it nowhere. Verification belongs on the server, in a library.

expiry.question: How do I know whether a token has expired?
expiry.answer: The exp claim in the payload is a count of seconds since the epoch. The tool compares it with your browser's clock and says so in one sentence at the top: still valid or expired, and when. If a token carries no exp at all, the tool says "no expiry claim" rather than "valid" — calling something valid that was never checked would be the wrong answer.

privacy.question: Is my token sent to a server?
privacy.answer: No. Decoding happens in your browser, and after the page has loaded this tool makes no network requests at all. The token is not stored either: refresh the page and it is gone.
